title: Travel
goal: Talk about a trip: verbs of movement take *sein*, not *haben* — plus two past forms used every day, *war* and *hatte*.
bekal: use *sein* + Partizip II for verbs of movement

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Wie war deine Reise?
dialogs.intro: Budi has just come back from Munich. Watch the helper verb in each sentence — some use *habe*, some use *bin*, and the difference is no accident.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Du bist zurück! Wie war deine Reise?
lines.id: You're back! How was your trip?
lines.literal: you are back! how was your trip?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sehr schön! Ich bin am Freitag nach München gefahren.
lines.id: Really nice! I went to Munich on Friday.
lines.literal: very nice! I am on Friday to Munich driven.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Mit dem Zug oder mit dem Flugzeug?
lines.literal: with the train or with the plane?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mit dem Zug. Die Fahrt hat sechs Stunden gedauert.
lines.id: By train. The journey took six hours.
lines.literal: with the train. the journey has six hours lasted.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Sechs Stunden! Was hast du im Zug gemacht?
lines.id: Six hours! What did you do on the train?
lines.literal: six hours! what have you in-the train made?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich habe gelesen und ich bin ein bisschen eingeschlafen.
lines.id: I read, and I fell asleep for a bit.
lines.literal: I have read and I am a bit fallen-asleep.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und in München? Wo bist du geblieben?
lines.id: And in Munich? Where did you stay?
lines.literal: and in Munich? where are you stayed?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bei einem Freund. Er ist letztes Jahr dorthin gezogen.
lines.id: With a friend. He moved there last year.
lines.literal: at a friend. he is last year there-to moved.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Am Samstag sind wir in die Berge gefahren. Wir sind drei Stunden gelaufen!
lines.id: On Saturday we went to the mountains. We walked for three hours!
lines.literal: on Saturday are we into the mountains driven. we are three hours walked!

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Drei Stunden? Warst du nicht müde?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Doch, sehr! Aber das Wetter war perfekt und ich hatte keine Wahl.
lines.id: Oh yes, very! But the weather was perfect and I had no choice.
lines.literal: oh-yes, very! but the weather was perfect and I had no choice.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: And when did you get back?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Gestern Abend. Ich bin um elf Uhr angekommen.
lines.id: Last night. I got in at eleven.
lines.literal: yesterday evening. I am at eleven o'clock arrived.

notes: ***sein* for movement and change.** *gefahren*, *gelaufen*, *gekommen*, *gezogen*, *eingeschlafen*, *angekommen* — all of these use *bin/bist/ist*, not *habe*. The rule: if the verb moves you from one place to another, or changes your state, the helper verb is *sein*.
***bleiben* takes *sein* even though there's no movement at all.** So does *sein* itself: *Ich bin in München **gewesen***. These two exceptions have no neat explanation — just memorize them.

**Line 4: *hat gedauert*.** *Dauern* (to last) takes *haben*, because nothing moves — it's time that passes. Verbs like this are easy to mix up; notice that what decides is not the topic (travel) but the verb itself.

***war* and *hatte*.** Lines 11 and 12 use the simple past of *sein* and *haben*, and this is the form people actually use: *Das Wetter **war** perfekt*, *Ich **hatte** keine Wahl*. The Perfekt forms (*ist gewesen*, *hat gehabt*) exist, but you rarely hear them.

***Doch!*** is a word English has no equivalent for: it answers **yes** to a question asked in the **negative**. *Warst du nicht müde?* → *Doch!* = "oh yes, I was". Answering *Ja* there would be confusing; answering *Nein* means you weren't tired.

**Line 10: *in die Berge gefahren*.** *In* + Akkusativ because there's movement — this is the other side of the table in unit 13. Compare: *Wir sind **in den** Bergen gewandert* (within the mountains, no direction) versus *Wir sind **in die** Berge gefahren* (heading there).

grammars.title: The Perfekt with sein
body: Roughly ten percent of German verbs form the Perfekt with *sein* instead of *haben*. All of them fall into one of the three groups below.
after: The form of *sein* follows the subject as usual: *ich bin*, *du bist*, *er ist*, *wir sind*, *ihr seid*, *sie/Sie sind*. If you know the table from unit 1, you've already mastered half of this chapter.

⚠️ Some verbs can take either, depending on whether there's movement: *Ich **bin** nach Berlin gefahren* (I went to Berlin) versus *Ich **habe** das Auto gefahren* (I drove the car). The second has an object, so it behaves like an ordinary verb.
Dictionaries mark this with **s.** or **h.**, or simply write *ist gefahren* / *hat gemacht*. Look out for that mark every time you note down a new verb.

grammars.title: war and hatte — two past forms you need
body: For all other verbs, Germans tell stories in the Perfekt. For *sein* and *haben*, though, they use the simple past — and so should you.

head: Person
sein → war
haben → hatte
Example
rows: Ich war müde. Ich hatte keine Zeit.

after: Notice a pattern you already know: *ich* and *er/sie/es* use **the same form with no ending** — just like the modal verbs in unit 11. This pattern holds for every simple-past form in German.

Two questions you'll ask again and again: ***Wie war…?*** ("how was…?") for anything in the past — *Wie war deine Reise?*, *Wie war dein Wochenende?*, *Wie war der Film?* And the answer: *Es war schön / interessant / anstrengend.*

blocks.text: ⚠️ *der See* (lake) and *die See* (sea) are spelled exactly the same and mean different things — only the article tells them apart. It's the clearest example of why learning a noun without its *der/die/das* means learning half a word.

sections.title: haben or sein? A quick test

blocks.text: Ask yourself one thing: **am I moving from one place to another?** If yes, *sein*. If I'm doing something to something, *haben*.

blocks.title: Write your own story
items: Pick a trip you've really taken — a visit home, a vacation, or just a trip out of town.
Write six sentences: when you left, how you traveled, how long it took, where you stayed, what you did, when you came back.
Check them one by one: which take *bin*, which take *habe*? Mistakes here are completely normal and disappear quickly once you've written it out yourself.
Ich bin am Freitag nach München gefahren.
Die Fahrt hat sechs Stunden gedauert.
Ich bin um elf Uhr angekommen.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order to make a past-tense sentence.
items: geblieben / bei einem Freund / ich / bin
gedauert / sechs Stunden / die Fahrt / hat
angekommen / ich / um elf Uhr / bin

answers: How was your trip? — I went to Munich on Friday. — The journey took six hours. — Where did you stay? — We walked for three hours. — I got in at eleven o'clock.
